changes.before: Change the format from %q to %s. What prints?
changes.after: Choose how a value appears as text.

before: fmt.Printf uses a format string. %d formats an integer in decimal; %q formats a quoted escaped representation for a String. %s prints String content without surrounding quotation marks.
The escape \n adds a newline. fmt.Println adds its own line ending and spaces between separate arguments.
Displaying a value as text does not change the stored value’s type.
Use a suitable formatting verb instead of assuming every verb means the same thing. Go can report formatting mismatch text; that is not correct data output.
Expected output or behavior: "moon". Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare content output and quoted output for a string containing a space or newline. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: `fmt.Printf` uses a format string to choose how values look. `%q` shows text with quotation marks and escapes special characters. `%s` shows the text itself. `%d` shows a whole number in ordinary decimal digits.
`\n` means start a new line. Printf needs it when you want a line ending. Println adds its own line ending.
Formatting changes how a value is displayed. It does not change the value stored in the variable.
Choose a format that fits the value. A wrong format can show an error-like message instead of the output you wanted.
The screen shows `"moon"`, including the quotation marks. That is what %q asks for.
Replace %q with %s in the same example. The stored text stays the same; only its display changes.
